results.note: Table I (IV reference dose) and the Table II continuation columns on p. 481, read from the page image, give t1/2 10.7 h (SD 2.39) and 10.7 h (SD 2.11) for the intranasal and smoked conditions and 11.8 h (SD 3.59) and 11.0 h (SD 2.68) for the IV reference dose, with CL 272 and 271 and Vss 4.30 and 4.02; all match. CL and Vss belong to the IV reference dose (the intranasal/smoked table has no such columns); Table VI on p. 482 prints 284 (SD 59.0) for the intranasal-session IV clearance, so the paper is inconsistent with itself on that one value.

Table 1 (p. 719) and Results (p. 718), read from page images because the text layer is garbled: half-lives 11.8 h (SE 1.35) and 13.1 h (SE 1.54), geometric means 11.1 and 12.2 h, range 8.3 to 18.2 h, total clearance 0.192 (SE 0.0097) L/h/kg and Vd 3.24 and 3.73 L/kg all match. The Vd row is in the same table but is not named in the locator.
Table 1 plasma block (p. 125): t1/2 9.3 h (SD 3.7) and 11.1 h (SD 7.2), Cmax 20.2 and 32.4 µg/L, tmax 5.4 h (SD 2.5) and 7.5 h (SD 3.4) for the 10 mg and 20 mg sustained-release doses; all match.

results.corrected_extracted: In the double-blind crossover, the half-life of intravenous d-methamphetamine was 10.2 h (SD 2.3), 10.3 h (SD 2.6) and 10.7 h (SD 2.6) in the three conditions containing it, against 13.6 h (SD 3.8), 13.3 h (SD 3.5) and 15.0 h (SD 4.6) for l-methamphetamine; clearance 0.257 to 0.266 against 0.188 to 0.221 L·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹. The mean volume of distribution (3.73 to 4.17 L/kg across all conditions) was not significantly different between the isomers (P = 0.2206).
results.corrected_locator: Table I, t½ and CL rows (all six dosing conditions) (pp. 410–411); Results › Pharmacokinetic results, 5th paragraph, volume-of-distribution sentence (p. 408, right column)
results.note: Table I (pp. 410-411) half-lives and clearances match for all six conditions, but the paper does not say the volume of distribution was the same: the Results (p. 408, right column) say the mean was 3.73 to 4.17 L/kg and not significantly different between the isomers (P = 0.2206). Wording corrected and the p. 408 sentence added to the locator.

Tables III and IV continuation columns (p. 481): amphetamine t1/2 16.2, 16.9, 15.2 and 16.3 h and AUC ratio to methamphetamine 15.5, 16.1, 19.3 and 17.8% across the four conditions; the stated ranges 15.2 to 16.9 h and 15.5 to 19.3% match.

Right column of p. 720 (page image): the elimination rate constant fell with absorbed dose (r² = 0.7042, p = 0.037) and the authors say the kinetics may be dose-dependent through a saturable renal process. The final clause (half-life belongs to the low dose range) is the encyclopedia's own inference, in line with the paper's hedge.

Table II on p. 480: intranasal Cmax 113 ng/mL (SD 23.1) at 2.66 h (SD 1.16) and smoked 50.9 (SD 24.7) at 2.47 h (SD 3.91) match. The 72-hour sampling is in the Methods (p. 477) and the no-placebo, simultaneous-IV design in the Methods and Discussion (p. 483), not on p. 480; that this laboratory is independent of the two other studies cannot be checked in this PDF.

Results at the foot of p. 1208 and top of p. 1209 and Figure 4: caudate/putamen 3.51 (SD 0.45) against 4.40 (SD 0.18) and nucleus accumbens 2.93 (SD 0.77) against 4.16 (SD 0.64), Mann-Whitney U = 1.0 and 8.5, p<0.001, and the 20.2% and 29.6% differences all match; 11 methamphetamine-only men against 9 comparison men.

Subjects section and Table 1 (p. 1207) and Results (p. 1208): 3 referring services, 8 of 11 with prior methamphetamine psychosis, use for 1 month to 15 years, 4 with earlier neuroleptic treatment, age 27.4 (SD 5.6) against 26.9 (SD 4.5) and education 11.5 against 11.8 years all match. No dose or frequency is tabulated; the Discussion (p. 1212) describes use only as recreational with no history of toxic or high-dose use.

results.corrected_extracted: In 11 men abstinent from 7 days to 1.5 years, dopamine transporter binding potential showed no significant correlation with the duration of abstinence in either the caudate/putamen or the nucleus accumbens, while in the same 11 men it correlated negatively with the duration of methamphetamine use (Kendall's tau −0.48, p<0.05, and −0.73, p<0.01). A non-significant rank correlation in 11 people is weak evidence either way. The authors, adding an earlier PET study of people abstinent for more than 3 years, say these findings suggest that a lasting reduction could occur after habitual use.
results.corrected_locator: Table 1, Duration of Abstinence column (p. 1207); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 1209); Figure 5 (p. 1211); Discussion, paragraph beginning 'We found no significant correlation between the duration of abstinence' (p. 1212)
results.note: Table 1 (p. 1207, abstinence 7 days to 1.5 years), p. 1209 (no significant correlation with abstinence; tau -0.48 and -0.73 for duration of use) and Figure 5 match. The authors do not say the reduction is long-lasting: the abstract says it may be, and the Discussion (p. 1212) says that, together with an earlier PET study of people abstinent for more than 3 years, the findings suggest a lasting reduction could occur. Replacement wording keeps the hedge and adds the Discussion paragraph and Figure 5 page to the place.

results.corrected_extracted: A previous study (reference 23) using the same PET scanner and tracer found a pronounced striatal dopamine transporter reduction of about 80% in unmedicated patients with Parkinson's disease, against a reduction of roughly 20% in the caudate/putamen of the methamphetamine group here, none of whom had symptoms of parkinsonism or other neurological abnormalities. The authors write that, because striatal dopamine transporter declines with age, people who use methamphetamine chronically may have a greater risk of developing Parkinson's disease as they age, and that in this group, as distinct from Parkinson's disease, the small reduction appears to have predictive value for psychiatric signs.
results.note: The Discussion paragraph on p. 1212 gives the 80% and 20% reductions and no parkinsonism, as stated. But the paper does not say a small reduction predicts psychiatric rather than motor signs: it says people who use methamphetamine chronically may have a greater risk of Parkinson's disease as they age, and that the small reduction appears to have predictive value for psychiatric signs. Replacement text restores both statements.

Methamphetamine overdose paragraphs on p. 1088 and the 4th paragraph on p. 1091 (after Table 3): feature lists, agitation about 20%, suicidal ideation 6-12%, acute psychosis 7-12%, rhabdomyolysis up to 14%, seizures 3-4%, cause-of-death list, the forensic-series remark, the guide-only remark on blood concentrations and the 94 000 emergency-department admissions all match. The remarks that no denominators or case-fatality figures are given are accurate for the text.

Methods (pp. 245-246, 248), Table 2 (p. 251) and the Discussion quotation (p. 265): response rate 82.4%, n = 8,098, stimulants 15.3% (SE 0.7) used, 1.7% (SE 0.3) dependent, 11.2% (SE 1.6) of people who had used them, and the other drug proportions match; the quote is word for word. The lay-interviewer detail is on p. 247, just outside the pages named, and the editors' 95% CI (11.2 +/- 1.96 x 1.6 = 8.1 to 14.3) is arithmetically right.

Results > Reinforcing effects (pp. 77-78): capsule chosen on a mean of 4.3 of 8 occasions at 5 mg and 4.4 at 10 mg against 1.4 and 1.3 under placebo (P<0.02 and P<0.01), no difference between the two active doses or the two placebo conditions; matches.

Participants paragraph (p. 76): 8 completers (1 woman, 7 men, age 23 to 42, mean 31.1), 3 with any methamphetamine history and 7 with cocaine, 11 started and 3 did not complete, one for difficulty sleeping in the 10 mg phase; matches.

Discussion paragraph on p. 80: vouchers chosen during approximately half of the choice opportunities under both active conditions (consistent with 4.3 and 4.4 of 8 capsule choices) and about 80% of the time under placebo, and the authors give an insufficiently broad dose range as a second likely reason for no dose effect; matches.

Abstract, Methods 2.2-2.4, Tables 1-4 and Results 3.1 all match, including 40,472 and 40,358 pairs, 51 vs 29 cases, HR 1.76 (1.12-2.76, p = 0.014), median age 57.2 vs 63.8, cocaine comparison 36 vs 15 with HR 2.41 (1.32-4.41) and cocaine vs appendicitis 20 vs 21 with HR 1.04 (0.56-1.93). The anchor's own flags on the abstract's 2.75, p = 0.017 and 2.44 are correct; the crude proportions are labelled as the editors' calculation.

Design (3rd paragraph) and fractional anisotropy (5th paragraph, Fig. 1B legend) on p. 602 and the grey-matter paragraph continuing on p. 603 match: F(2,141) = 26.3, permutation P = 0.004; putamen P = 0.013, posterior insula P = 0.012, amygdala P = 0.144. The 3-column layout of p. 603 was read column 1 to 3 on the page image, which puts the permutation values in the 7th paragraph as the locator says; the supplement was not read, as the anchor states.

Table II continuation columns (p. 481): F 79.4% (SD 13.1) for the intranasal and 37.4% (SD 14.2) for the smoked condition, computed against the simultaneous 10 mg deuterated IV infusion (Table I and II titles); matches.

Results > Pharmacokinetic measures (p. 479, 2nd paragraph, running from the left to the right column): 22.2 mg (SD 8.4) extracted from 40 mg, range 11.3 to 36.4 mg (28%-91%), 67% on the estimated delivered dose and 37% on the loaded dose; intranasal higher on nominal doses (P<.02) but not on delivered dose (P<.1). All match.

Results p. 718 (26.9%, SE 1.0, left in the pipe; 21.8 mg, SE 0.33; 90.3% bioavailability) and Table 1 p. 719 (Dose 21.8, SE 0.33; f 0.903, SE 0.104), read from page images; values are SE per the Methods. The 'Smoking Efficiency and Dose' paragraph lies wholly on p. 718, so 'continuing on p. 719' applies only to the Table 1 rows.

Table 1 tmax (p. 125) and the Discussion on p. 128 match: 5.4 h (SD 2.5) and 7.5 h (SD 3.4), against 2.9 to 3.6 h for other oral formulations. The same paragraph says one study using the same sustained-release formulation reported a shorter tmax of 3.0 h, possibly because of more frequent sampling, which the anchor does not mention.

results.corrected_extracted: Peak subjective effect came at an average of 18 min (SE 2.1) from the start of vapor inhalation, a figure the authors cite to their earlier report, and at 17.4 min (SE 1.1) after intravenous injection; the maximum heart-rate change came at 11.8 min (SE 1.6) and 12.6 min (SE 2.8). Figure 3, which plots subjective effect against plasma concentration, shows the effects subsiding while plasma concentrations were still high.
results.corrected_locator: Results, 1st–2nd paragraphs (left column of p. 720, last sentence at the top of the right column); Figure 3
results.note: The peak-effect times (18 min, SE 2.1, cited to the authors' earlier report; 17.4 min, SE 1.1) and heart-rate times (11.8 min, SE 1.6; 12.6 min, SE 2.8) match, but the clause 'well before the plasma peak measured for the non-injection routes' is not in this paper: Cook measured smoked and IV conditions only. What the paper says at this place is that Figure 3 shows effects subsiding while plasma concentrations were still high; replacement text says that. The heart-rate sentence ends at the top of the right column of p. 720.

results.corrected_extracted: Half-life of intravenous d-methamphetamine 10.2 h (SD 2.3), 10.3 (SD 2.6) and 10.7 (SD 2.6) against l-methamphetamine 13.6 (SD 3.8), 13.3 (SD 3.5) and 15.0 (SD 4.6); clearance 0.257 to 0.266 against 0.188 to 0.221 L·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹; volume of distribution 3.73 to 4.17 L/kg across all conditions, not significantly different between the isomers (P = 0.2206); amphetamine-to-methamphetamine AUC ratio 0.162 to 0.173 for the d-isomer against 0.029 to 0.038 for the l-isomer.
results.corrected_locator: Table I, t½, CL, Vd and amphetamine rows (all six dosing conditions) (pp. 410–411); Results › Pharmacokinetic results, 5th paragraph, volume-of-distribution sentence (p. 408, right column)
results.note: Table I numbers match for all six conditions (half-lives, clearances, Vd 3.73 to 4.17 L/kg, amphetamine AUC ratios 0.162 to 0.173 and 0.029 to 0.038), but 'the same volume of distribution' overstates the paper, which reports no significant difference between the isomers (P = 0.2206, p. 408 right column). Wording corrected and the p. 408 sentence added to the locator.

Methods p. 407 (80% to 125% criterion) and Results p. 408, left column: AUC ratios 0.910 (0.837-0.983), 0.894 (0.821-0.967) and 0.679 (0.622-0.736), with the l-isomer AUC 30% greater after the racemate (P = .0085); all match. The ratios are in the 2nd paragraph only; the 3rd paragraph (Cmax) is not used.

Table II (p. 414, column order placebo, l 0.25, l 0.5, racemic, d 0.25, d 0.5): systolic 34.5 (18.9), 33.4 (17.8), 19.5 (11.3), 4.3 (9.9); visual-analogue intoxication 46.0 (35.3), 24.7 (27.4), 30.3 (24.9), 1.7 (4.7); monetary value $14.60, $10.70, $11.30, $1.10 all match for the d 0.5, racemic, l 0.5 and placebo conditions.

Results > Physiologic measures on p. 409 (paragraph running on from p. 408): all conditions peaked at about 5 to 15 minutes, values returned to baseline between 2 and 4 hours after either dose of l-methamphetamine, and d-methamphetamine effects persisted up to 6 hours (Fig 4). Matches; the 1-minute infusion is from the Methods.

results.corrected_extracted: The abstract says 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine produced peak intoxication (46.0 SD 35.3 versus 30.3 SD 24.9) and drug-liking (47.7 SD 35.1 versus 28.6 SD 24.8) ratings similar to the same dose of d-methamphetamine; the pairs are printed with the d-isomer's value first, so the sentence reads as if the larger value were the l-isomer's. Table II gives the peak means as 46.0 (SD 35.3) for 0.5 mg/kg d-methamphetamine against 30.3 (SD 24.9) for 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine on intoxication and 47.7 (SD 35.1) against 28.6 (SD 24.8) on drug liking, with no mark for a significant difference between them at peak; the Results say few significant differences were found among the peak effects of the active doses other than 0.25 mg/kg l-methamphetamine. In the Results paragraph on ratings across time, the 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine dose produced significantly smaller effects than the same dose of d-methamphetamine on intoxication, any drug effect and drug liking (P<0.0001), and its effects approached baseline at about 3 hours while doses containing d-methamphetamine stayed intoxicating for up to 6 hours.
results.corrected_locator: Abstract, Results sentence on l-methamphetamine (p. 403); Results › Pharmacodynamic measures › Subjective measures, 2nd–3rd paragraphs (p. 410); Table II, visual analog scales block (p. 414)
results.note: The abstract (p. 403) and Table II (p. 414) values are as stated, but 'the Results report the l-isomer's effects as significantly smaller' needs its context: the p. 410 text gives that difference (P<.0001) in the paragraph on ratings across time, whereas Table II carries no mark for a d versus l difference at peak and the text says few peak differences were significant. The final sentence ('the claim follows the table, not the abstract') is the encyclopedia's own remark, not the paper's, so it is dropped; p. 410 added to the place.

Results, 1st-2nd paragraphs on p. 720 (page image): peak effect at 18 min (SE 2.1; cited to the authors' earlier report) and 17.4 min (SE 1.1), heart rate at 11.8 (SE 1.6) and 12.6 min (SE 2.8), Fig. 3 'effects subsided, whereas plasma concentrations were still high', and cardiovascular measures back to baseline within a short period after both routes; matches. The abstract also says effects subsided before marked falls in plasma concentration, suggesting acute tolerance.

Last paragraph of p. 719 into p. 720: 38% (SE 9.8) for smoking (cited to ref. 4) and 41.5% (SE 20.1) for IV injection, relative to the maximum each subject had previously experienced; matches. That the smoked values come from the same six volunteers is an inference (they are cited to the earlier report and the abstract says the same volunteers received the IV dose), not a statement in the paper.

Results > Physiologic measures on p. 409 and Figure 4 (p. 413): all conditions peaked at about 5 to 15 minutes, l-methamphetamine effects returned to baseline between 2 and 4 hours and d-methamphetamine effects persisted up to 6 hours; matches.

Table I t1/2 row (pp. 410-411): d-methamphetamine 10.2 h (SD 2.3), 10.3 (SD 2.6) and 10.7 (SD 2.6) match. The conclusion that well over half the drug remained when effects ended is an inference from t1/2 and the effect duration (up to 6 hours, about two-thirds remaining at a 10.3 h half-life), consistent with Fig. 2A.

Results > Food intake (p. 79, page image) and Fig. 4: reductions of about 43% (5 mg) and 37% (10 mg), P<0.01 in the text; fat, carbohydrate and protein fell in a similar pattern; fewer eating occasions and longer gaps for 5 mg, smaller intake per occasion for 10 mg (P<0.01); matches. The Fig. 4 legend gives P<0.03 for the same comparison.

Table 1 (p. 79, page image): Hungry 11.46 (SEM 3.94) after the 10 mg sample dose against 26.50 (SEM 7.18) after placebo, listed under items methamphetamine decreased (F 12.63, all F significant at P<0.03); matches. The locator also names the Sedated row, which the anchor does not use.

Discussion paragraph on p. 80: reduction of approximately 1415 kcal relative to placebo, and an earlier study from the same laboratory with reductions of approximately 1150 and 1450 kcal; matches. The earlier study (Comer et al. 2001, repeated twice-daily dosing) shares authors with this paper per the reference list, and its figures are second-hand here.
